column3: The Hebrew speaks of David’s days drawing near and explicitly introduces his speech.
The Hebrew says to become a man; BSB has “prove yourself a man.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew names his “word” and the sons’ guarding “their way”; BSB has “promise” and taking heed to walk. It describes the unfailing line with the image of a man not being cut off.
The Hebrew says he placed war-blood in peace, without a separate verb for avenging. The sandal is singular.
The Hebrew describes Solomon bringing the gray hair down, rather than letting it go down.
The Hebrew says they drew near to him; BSB has “stood by me.”
The Hebrew introduces Shimei with “behold” rather than a command to keep an eye on him. It pairs cursing with a grievous curse and says “I will not kill you” without a separate “never.”
The Hebrew joins knowing what to do and bringing the gray hair down with “and”; BSB makes the latter a purpose.
The Hebrew says David lay down with his fathers; BSB has “rested.”
The Hebrew describes the reign as days and repeats reigning for each city.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew’s answer is simply “Peace”; BSB adds “Yes.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says all Israel set their faces toward him; BSB renders this as expecting him to reign.
The Hebrew says not to turn away his face; BSB has “do not deny me.” Her answer is simply “Speak.”
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed; BSB supplies Adonijah. It again uses the image of not turning away the face.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says the king placed a throne for his mother; BSB expresses this as having one brought.
The Hebrew repeats not turning away the face in both request and answer; BSB uses denying.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed; BSB supplies Bathsheba.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew oath says “thus may God do to me, and thus may He add”; BSB makes punishment and severity explicit. The request is called “this word.”
The Hebrew says he made him a house and spoke; BSB interprets the house as a dynasty and the speaking as promising.
The Hebrew preserves the hand of Benaiah and leaves both the struck man and the object of sending unnamed; BSB supplies Adonijah and “the order.”
The Hebrew calls him a “man of death,” says “this day,” and has no separate “back” in the command to go.
The Hebrew describes fulfillment as the purpose of expelling Abiathar; BSB states the resulting fulfillment.
The Hebrew names Joab three times; BSB names him once and uses pronouns for the later occurrences.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves Joab unnamed in the exchange and repeats “thus” for his speaking and answering; BSB names him and condenses the final report.
